uni-fin-bank-actuarial.title: Banking operations, careers and actuarial basics
uni-fin-bank-actuarial.description: How banks actually run (deposits, lending, NPAs, reconciliation), how to build a banking career, and the foundations of actuarial science: life tables, present values and pricing. Educational overviews, not professional advice.

courses.title: Banking operations: deposits, lending, NPAs and reconciliation
courses.summary: The bank's balance sheet and the ratios that describe its health, with reconciliation practice.
outcomes: Compute CASA, NIM and gross NPA ratios
Explain reserves and the money multiplier model
Reconcile a cash book with a bank statement

scenes.text: A branch manager presents three numbers: CASA, NIM and gross NPA.
A trainee must compute them.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice. Figures are fictional practice numbers.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: CASA ratio = (current + savings deposits) ÷ total deposits. NIM = (interest earned − interest paid) ÷ average earning assets. Gross NPA ratio = gross NPAs ÷ gross advances. A loan is generally classified an NPA when overdue for more than 90 days.

activity.prompt: Interest earned ₹9,000 cr, paid ₹5,500 cr, average earning assets ₹50,000 cr. NIM %?

lessons.title: Lab: Reserves and the money multiplier model

scenes.text: ₹100 is deposited. The bank lends most of it, which returns as new deposits.
A simplified model shows the chain.

steps.title: RBI tools
steps.body: RBI uses the repo rate, reserve requirements such as CRR (cash reserve ratio) and SLR (statutory liquidity ratio), and other tools to manage liquidity and inflation.

steps.title: Simplified multiplier
steps.body: If reserves held are 4% (a hypothetical CRR), the textbook multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.04 = 25, so ₹100 could support up to ₹2,500 of deposits in the model. Real banks leak cash and hold extra reserves, so reality is far lower.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: This is a classroom model, not a forecast.

activity.prompt: Reserve ratio 4% (hypothetical). Money multiplier?

scenes.text: The firm's cash book shows ₹1,20,000 but the bank statement shows ₹1,14,500.
A clerk must find the difference.

steps.title: Common differences
steps.body: Cheques issued but not yet cleared; deposits in transit; bank charges and interest not yet in the cash book.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Bank balance 1,14,500 + deposits in transit 9,000 − uncleared cheques 3,500 = 1,20,000, matching the cash book.

steps.title: Control
steps.body: Reconcile monthly and investigate unexplained items immediately.

activity.prompt: Bank statement ₹1,14,500; deposits in transit ₹9,000; uncleared cheques ₹3,500. Adjusted bank balance (₹)?

questions.q: Reconciliation: bank 50,000, outstanding cheques 4,000, in transit 6,000?

courses.title: Banking careers: roles, exams and skills
courses.summary: Clerical, officer, specialist and compliance paths in banking, and how to prepare. Exam names are used nominatively; check official notices.

scenes.text: Nisha wants to join a bank but is unsure which role fits.
She sorts roles.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational; vacancies, eligibility and exam patterns change, so read official notifications. No affiliation with any bank or exam body.

steps.title: Families
steps.body: Clerical/customer-service, probationary officers and managers, specialist officers (IT, risk, credit, treasury, law), and compliance/audit.

steps.title: Skills
steps.body: Numeracy, communication, integrity and regulatory awareness matter in all roles.

activity.prompt: Match the role to its core work.
pairs: Manages bank's funds and market positions

scenes.text: A customer says someone asked for his OTP and he shared it.
Money has just left his account.

steps.title: Priority
steps.body: Block the card/UPI/net banking immediately, record details, escalate to the fraud team, and guide him to report on the national cyber helpline 1930 and cybercrime portal.

steps.title: Tone
steps.body: Be calm and non-judgmental; speed matters.

steps.title: Reporting
steps.body: Prompt reporting improves the chance of limiting loss; liability rules depend on RBI customer-protection guidelines and timing.

a.text: A customer reports a fraudulent debit minutes ago. What first?

choices.label: Block the channels and log the complaint

b.text: Fraud team alerted; customer told about 1930 and the cybercrime portal.

c.text: Funds moved on; the customer loses trust.

scenes.text: Nisha plans for a recruitment exam.
She divides topics and tests.

steps.title: Typical sections
steps.body: Quantitative aptitude, reasoning, English, banking and general awareness; some exams have interviews. Check each notification.

steps.title: Time maths
steps.body: 6 months ≈ 26 weeks; 4 study weeks per topic block, 1 mock per week.

steps.title: Scams
steps.body: No one can guarantee a bank job for a fee.

activity.prompt: Plan tasks.
items: Read banking and financial news daily

courses.title: Actuarial science I: probability, life tables and present value
courses.summary: Mortality rates from a life table, time value and a single-premium calculation. Independent introduction; actuarial qualifications are set by professional bodies such as the Institute of Actuaries of India.
outcomes: Compute q_x from a life table
Discount a payment with a discount factor
Compute a one-year term net single premium

scenes.text: A hypothetical table starts with 90,000 living at age 60 and 89,100 at age 61.
An analyst asks what fraction died.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational. The table is hypothetical and not real mortality data.

steps.title: Notation
steps.body: l_x = number alive at age x; d_x = deaths between x and x+1; q_x = d_x ÷ l_x.

options: Probability of dying within a year

lessons.title: Lab: Present value of an annuity

scenes.text: A trust will pay ₹1,000 at the end of each of 3 years.
At 5% interest, what is it worth today?

steps.title: Discounting
steps.body: v = 1 ÷ (1+i). PV of an annuity-immediate = P × (1 − v^n) ÷ i.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: The PV must be below the undiscounted total of ₹3,000.

activity.prompt: ₹1,000 at end of each of 3 years, 5% interest. PV (₹, 2 decimals)?

quiz.q: PV is than the total paid?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – one-year term net single premium

scenes.text: An insurer sells a one-year term policy of ₹10,00,000 to a person with q = 0.002.
What is the pure (net) premium at 5% interest?

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: Net single premium = benefit × q × v (benefit paid at end of year). This excludes expenses, profit and risk margins.

steps.title: Real pricing
steps.body: Real premiums add loadings, use real tables and regulatory assumptions.

activity.prompt: Benefit ₹10,00,000, q = 0.002, interest 5%. Net single premium (₹, 2 decimals)?

questions.q: PV of ₹1,100 due in 1 year at 10%?
Net single premium: benefit 5,00,000, q 0.004, i 5%?

courses.title: Actuarial science II: frequency, severity and pricing
courses.summary: General-insurance pricing: pure premium, loadings, loss and combined ratios.
outcomes: Compute pure premium from frequency and severity

scenes.text: An insurer sees 5 claims per 100 policies a year, averaging ₹40,000.
What is the expected claim cost per policy?

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational. Numbers are hypothetical.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: Pure premium = claim frequency × average severity.

activity.prompt: Frequency 0.05, severity ₹40,000. Pure premium (₹)?

lessons.title: Lab: Loadings and the gross premium

scenes.text: Selling and running a policy costs money.
The insurer loads 25% of the gross premium for expenses and profit.

steps.title: Gross-up
steps.body: If loadings are a share L of the gross premium, gross = pure ÷ (1 − L).

steps.title: Why not ×1.25
steps.body: Because 25% is of the gross premium, not of the pure premium.

activity.prompt: Pure ₹2,000, loadings 25% of gross. Gross premium (₹, 2 decimals)?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – loss ratio and combined ratio

scenes.text: An insurer earns premium ₹1,000 crore and pays claims of ₹700 crore, with expenses of ₹250 crore.
Is the underwriting profitable?

steps.title: Ratios
steps.body: Loss ratio = claims ÷ premium. Expense ratio = expenses ÷ premium. Combined ratio = their sum; below 100% means underwriting profit before investment income.

steps.title: Investment income
steps.body: Insurers also earn investment income on float, so a combined ratio slightly above 100% can still be profitable overall.

activity.prompt: Premium ₹1,000 cr, claims ₹700 cr, expenses ₹250 cr. Combined ratio %?

questions.q: Gross premium greater than pure because of?

uni-fin-cfa.title: CFA®-level concepts: independent practice
uni-fin-cfa.description: Independent, original practice material on CFA®-level topics: time value of money and statistics, financial statement analysis, corporate finance, valuation, portfolio theory and ethics. Not affiliated with or endorsed by CFA Institute; check the official curriculum. Educational, not investment advice.

courses.title: Quantitative methods: time value of money and statistics
courses.summary: Present value, NPV, mean and sample standard deviation with fully worked calculations. CFA® is a registered trademark of CFA Institute; this course is independent.
outcomes: Compute mean and sample standard deviation

scenes.text: A bond-like contract pays ₹1,00,000 in five years. The discount rate is 8%.
An analyst wants today's value.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice, and independent of CFA Institute. CFA® is a registered trademark of CFA Institute.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n.

activity.prompt: FV ₹1,00,000, 8% a year, 5 years. PV (₹, nearest rupee)?

scenes.text: A machine costs ₹1,000 and returns ₹400, ₹500, ₹600 over three years.
The required return is 10%.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: NPV = Σ CF_t ÷ (1+r)^t − initial outlay. Accept if NPV > 0 (in simple textbook cases).

steps.title: Estimates
steps.body: Cash flows and r are estimates; run sensitivity tests.

activity.prompt: Outlay 1,000; cash flows 400, 500, 600; r = 10%. NPV (2 decimals)?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – mean and sample standard deviation

scenes.text: A fund returned +10%, −5% and +15% in three years.
The analyst measures average and variability.

steps.title: Why n−1
steps.body: Dividing by n−1 corrects the bias when estimating from a sample.

steps.title: Caution
steps.body: Three data points are too few for conclusions; this is a calculation drill.

activity.prompt: Returns 10, −5, 15 (%). Sample standard deviation (2 decimals)?

courses.title: Financial statement analysis: inventory methods, DuPont and coverage
courses.summary: FIFO vs LIFO effects, the DuPont breakdown of ROE and interest coverage.

scenes.text: A trader buys 100 units at ₹10 then 100 at ₹12 and sells 100 for ₹15 each.
Profit depends on the inventory method.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice, and independent of CFA Institute. Accounting rules (such as Ind AS and IFRS) differ on whether LIFO is allowed.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: FIFO assumes the oldest units are sold first; LIFO assumes the latest are sold first.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Sales 1,500. FIFO COGS 1,000 → gross profit 500. LIFO COGS 1,200 → gross profit 300.

activity.prompt: Sell 100 at ₹15 after buying 100@₹10 then 100@₹12. FIFO gross profit (₹)?

quiz.q: In rising costs FIFO profit is?

scenes.text: A company has net margin 10%, asset turnover 1.5× and equity multiplier 2×.
ROE is the product.

steps.title: Identity
steps.body: ROE = net margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier.

steps.title: Leverage
steps.body: High ROE from leverage is riskier than from margins or turnover.

activity.prompt: Margin 10%, turnover 1.5, equity multiplier 2. ROE %?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – interest coverage and a red-flag review

scenes.text: A lender sees EBIT of ₹300 crore and interest of ₹60 crore.
She also notices receivables rising faster than sales.

steps.title: Coverage
steps.body: Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ interest = 300/60 = 5×.

steps.title: Quality checks
steps.body: Compare cash flow from operations with net income; rising receivables or inventory vs sales can signal aggressive recognition.

steps.title: Not accusation
steps.body: Red flags prompt questions, not conclusions.

activity.prompt: EBIT ₹300 crore; interest ₹60 crore. Interest coverage (×)?

questions.q: Rising costs: LIFO profit vs FIFO?
FIFO closing inventory in rising costs?

courses.title: Corporate finance: WACC and capital structure
courses.summary: Cost of capital with the tax shield, and decision rules for projects.

scenes.text: A firm pays 8% on debt and faces a 25% tax rate.
Interest is tax-deductible.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice, and independent of CFA Institute.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: After-tax cost of debt = pre-tax cost × (1 − tax rate).

activity.prompt: Pre-tax debt cost 8%, tax rate 25%. After-tax cost %?

scenes.text: A firm is 60% equity at a 12% cost and 40% debt at 6% after tax.
What is its weighted cost?

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: WACC = Σ weight × cost.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: Projects with returns above WACC (and similar risk) may add value.

activity.prompt: 60% equity at 12%, 40% debt at 6% after tax. WACC %?

scenes.text: A firm with WACC 9.6% sees projects returning 8%, 10% and 14%.
Which clear the hurdle?

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Accept projects whose IRR exceeds the cost of capital for their risk, subject to capital limits.

steps.title: Real life
steps.body: Strategic fit, uncertainty and financing constraints also matter.

steps.title: Estimates
steps.body: IRR depends on forecasts.

activity.prompt: Sort projects against a 9.6% hurdle.

questions.q: Interest tax shield value for debt 100 at 10%, tax 30%?

courses.title: Valuation, portfolio theory and ethics
courses.summary: Dividend discount model, bond pricing, portfolio return/risk, CAPM and an ethics scenario.
outcomes: Value a perpetuity-growth stock and a bond

lessons.title: Lab: Gordon growth and bond price

scenes.text: A stock expects a ₹6 dividend next year growing at 6% forever; required return 12%.
A 3-year 8% bond is discounted at 10%.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice, and independent of CFA Institute. Models are only as good as their inputs.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Gordon: P0 = D1 ÷ (r − g). Bond price = Σ coupon/(1+y)^t + face/(1+y)^n.

activity.prompt: Face 1,000, coupon 8%, 3 years, yield 10%. Bond price (₹, 2 decimals)?

quiz.q: Yield above coupon: price vs face?

lessons.title: Lab: Portfolio return, risk and CAPM

scenes.text: A 50/50 portfolio of assets with volatilities 20% and 10% and correlation 0.5.
Diversification lowers risk below the average.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: E(Rp) = Σ w·E(R). σp² = w1²σ1² + w2²σ2² + 2w1w2ρσ1σ2. CAPM: E(R) = rf + β(ERP).

steps.title: Assumptions
steps.body: Inputs are hypothetical and models simplify reality.

activity.prompt: 50/50 portfolio, σ 20% and 10%, ρ 0.5. Portfolio σ (%, 2 decimals)?

scenes.text: An analyst overhears that a listed client will announce a takeover tomorrow.
A friend asks if he should buy the stock.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: Material non-public information must not be used or passed on; trading on it is insider trading, prohibited in India by SEBI regulations.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Stop, do not trade or tip, tell compliance and document.

steps.title: Law
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

a.text: You hold unpublished price-sensitive information about a listed company. A friend asks for a hint. What do you do?

choices.label: Say nothing, avoid trading and inform compliance

b.text: Compliance records it and restricts the stock.

c.text: You face regulatory and career risk.

uni-fin-fintech-scams.title: Fintech & payments in India, and avoiding financial scams
uni-fin-fintech-scams.description: UPI, NPCI and RBI's role in general terms, digital lending and data-sharing basics, then hands-on scam defence: UPI/OTP fraud, fake investment schemes and loan apps, and what to do in the first hour. General education; rules and limits change, so verify with official sources. Not legal or investment advice.

courses.title: UPI and NPCI: how a payment really travels
courses.summary: Who does what in a UPI payment: apps, banks, NPCI and the PIN. In general terms; limits and rules change.
outcomes: Order the steps of a UPI payment
Explain why the PIN is only for paying

scenes.text: Arya scans a QR at a tea stall and pays ₹20.
In seconds the stall's bank account is credited. What happened between?

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not financial or legal advice. Limits, charges and rules change; check your bank, NPCI and RBI for current details.

steps.title: Players
steps.body: NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India) runs the UPI network. Your app (a TPAP) is the interface; your bank (the remitter) debits you; the stall's bank (beneficiary) credits it. UPI was launched in 2016.

steps.title: PIN
steps.body: You enter your UPI PIN only to PAY or authorise a debit, never to receive money.

activity.prompt: Order the payment journey.
items: Arya scans the stall's QR and enters the amount
The app sends the request to NPCI's UPI switch
Arya enters her UPI PIN to authorise
Her bank checks funds and debits her
The stall's bank is credited and both get confirmation

options: Umbrella body for retail payment systems
quiz.why: Set up with RBI and banks.

lessons.title: Lab: Pay request vs collect request

scenes.text: A buyer says 'I will send you ₹5,000' and sends a collect request instead.
Ria sees a screen asking for her PIN.

steps.title: Read the screen
steps.body: If the screen says you will PAY or asks for your PIN, money will leave your account. A genuine incoming payment needs no action from you.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: If you have to enter a PIN to receive money, it is a scam.

steps.title: Manage
steps.body: Review pending collect requests in your app and decline unknown ones.

a.text: A stranger says he sent ₹5,000 by mistake and asks you to 'approve' a request on your app. What do you do?

choices.label: Approve and enter PIN to receive it
Decline; check your bank balance; ask him to ask his bank

b.text: No money left your account and you reported the number.

c.text: ₹5,000 left your account; call your bank and 1930 now.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – the merchant fee arithmetic

scenes.text: A shop accepts cards and UPI and wonders why it pays fees on one but often not the other.
A student computes a hypothetical card fee.

steps.title: MDR
steps.body: Merchant discount rate (MDR) is the fee a merchant pays on a transaction. Card MDR is a percentage; policy on UPI MDR has been set by the government and may change. The rates here are assumptions.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Assumed card MDR 0.4% on ₹2,000 = ₹8. Merchant receives ₹1,992.

steps.title: Ecosystem
steps.body: Other NPCI products include IMPS, RuPay, BBPS (bill payments) and FASTag. Check NPCI for details.

activity.prompt: Assumed card MDR 0.4% on a ₹2,000 sale. Fee (₹)?

courses.title: RBI's role: payment systems, KYC and customer protection
courses.summary: What RBI regulates in payments, how NEFT/RTGS/IMPS differ in general terms, KYC and liability rules in general terms.
outcomes: Distinguish NEFT, RTGS and IMPS in general terms
State the customer-liability idea for unauthorised transactions

scenes.text: Kabir must pay ₹8 lakh for a flat booking and ₹500 to a friend.
He wonders which method suits each.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not financial or legal advice. Limits and timings change; confirm with your bank.

steps.title: Rails in general terms
steps.body: RTGS: large-value, real-time gross settlement, with a minimum amount. NEFT: batch-based transfers, available around the clock. IMPS and UPI: instant retail payments. The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 gives RBI the power to regulate payment systems.

steps.title: Always
steps.body: Verify the beneficiary account before sending a large payment.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the usual rail.

quiz.q: Law that empowers RBI over payment systems?

scenes.text: A caller says Tara's account will be blocked unless she updates KYC on a link.
Her bank branch says no such call was made.

steps.title: What KYC is
steps.body: KYC (know your customer) is identity verification required by RBI-regulated entities to prevent fraud and money laundering. Banks do it at the branch, via video KYC or their app.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Banks do not ask for your PIN, OTP, CVV or password by phone or link.

steps.title: Verify
steps.body: Call the number on your bank's official site or card, not the caller's number.

activity.prompt: Sort each message.

items.text: 'Share OTP to keep your account active'
'Visit branch with ID to update KYC'
Link to 'update KYC' from an unknown number
In-app notice asking to complete KYC

quiz.q: Banks ask your OTP by phone?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – the first-hour liability ladder

scenes.text: Tara sees a ₹12,000 debit she did not make.
How quickly she reports it matters.

steps.title: General idea
steps.body: RBI's customer-protection framework says that for unauthorised electronic transactions caused by bank-side lapses or third-party breaches reported promptly (within three working days), customer liability is zero; later reporting may carry limited liability as per the bank's board-approved policy. Details are in RBI's circular and your bank's policy.

steps.title: Act
steps.body: Block the card/UPI/net banking, note the time, report to the bank in writing, then to 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in.

steps.title: Escalation
steps.body: If the bank does not resolve it, RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme exists for complaints. This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Order the response.
items: Block cards, UPI and net banking
Call the bank and get a complaint number
Send a written complaint to the bank
Escalate to the bank's nodal officer and then the RBI ombudsman if unresolved

courses.title: Digital lending and data sharing: what is safe and lawful
courses.summary: APR arithmetic, key fact statements, RBI's digital-lending principles in general terms and the Account Aggregator idea.
outcomes: Compute an effective annual rate for a short loan
List red flags of illegal loan apps

lessons.title: Lab: The real cost of a 7-day loan

scenes.text: An app offers ₹10,000 for 7 days but deducts a 15% fee upfront.
Pranav gets ₹8,500 and must repay ₹10,000.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not financial or legal advice.

steps.title: Cost
steps.body: Fee = 1,500 on 8,500 received = 17.65% for 7 days. Annualised simple rate = 17.65% × 365/7 ≈ 920%.

activity.prompt: Receive ₹8,500, repay ₹10,000 after 7 days. Annualised simple rate % (nearest 10)?

lessons.title: Lab: Spot the illegal loan app

scenes.text: An app asks for access to Pranav's contacts and gallery.
Later, collectors message his friends.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: Unregistered lender, demand for contacts/gallery access, no clear lender name or key fact statement, funds routed via third-party accounts, threats and harassment.

steps.title: RBI principles in general terms
steps.body: RBI's digital-lending directions emphasise disclosure of costs, disbursal and repayment directly between the borrower's bank account and the regulated lender, and limits on data collection. Check RBI's published list of digital lending apps.

steps.title: Harassment
steps.body: Harassment and threats are crimes; report to 1930, cybercrime.gov.in and police (112).

activity.prompt: Sort app behaviours.

items.text: Shows lender name and key fact statement
Funds credited from an unknown personal account
Money disbursed directly to your bank account by a regulated entity

scenes.text: A lender offers to fetch Pranav's bank statements digitally through an Account Aggregator.
He sees a consent screen.

steps.title: Account Aggregator
steps.body: Account Aggregators are RBI-regulated entities that move your financial data between institutions only with your explicit, revocable consent; they do not read or store the data.

steps.title: Check consent
steps.body: Read what data, for how long, for what purpose, and who gets it.

steps.title: Never
steps.body: Do not share bank statements and passwords through chat with strangers.

activity.prompt: Before you consent, check:
items: Who is asking for the data
That I can revoke consent later

quiz.q: Share statements with strangers on chat?

courses.title: Scams I: UPI, OTP, KYC calls and fake support
courses.summary: Recognise and defeat phishing, vishing, fake customer-care numbers, screen-share apps and 'digital arrest' threats.

scenes.text: A caller claims to be from a courier and says a parcel with illegal items is in Meena's name.
He says police will arrest her unless she pays now.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not legal advice. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Tactics
steps.body: Urgency, fear of arrest, authority (police, bank, courier, 'CBI'), secrecy ('do not tell family') and requests to move money or share screen. No real agency arrests people over a video call or demands payment into a personal account; 'digital arrest' does not exist as a legal process.

steps.title: Routine
steps.body: Pause, hang up, verify on a number you look up yourself, and tell a family member.

activity.prompt: Sort the tactics.

items.text: 'Pay now or be arrested on video call'
'Do not tell anyone, this is confidential'
Bank sends a notification and asks you to visit a branch
'Install this screen-share app to fix your account'

options: A scam, not a legal process

lessons.title: Lab: Fake customer-care and screen-share traps

scenes.text: Ishaan searches for his bank's helpline and calls the first number he finds.
The 'agent' asks him to install a remote-access app.

steps.title: Why it happens
steps.body: Scammers buy ads or post fake numbers. Use the number printed on your card or on the bank's official app or site.

steps.title: Remote access
steps.body: Remote-control or screen-share apps let a stranger see OTPs and approve payments. Never install them for a 'support agent'.

steps.title: If done
steps.body: Uninstall, turn off internet, call your bank from another phone, block channels.

a.text: A 'support agent' asks you to install a screen-share app and read the code. What do you do?

choices.label: Install it to get help quickly
Refuse, hang up, call the number on your card

b.text: The real bank confirms no issue and notes the fraud number.

c.text: The caller drains your account; call 1930 and your bank immediately.

options: On your card or official app

scenes.text: Meena realises she paid ₹25,000 to a fake 'officer'.
She follows a drill.

steps.title: Drill
steps.body: Call 1930 and your bank, block UPI/cards, report on cybercrime.gov.in, keep screenshots and transaction IDs, file an FIR if advised.

steps.title: Freeze quickly
steps.body: Fast reporting can allow banks to hold funds in transit.

steps.title: Help
steps.body: Emergency 112. For stress after a scam, Tele-MANAS 14416 offers free support. This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Order the drill.
items: Stay calm and stop all further payments
Call 1930 and your bank to block and report
Save screenshots, numbers and transaction IDs
File a police complaint or FIR if advised

questions.q: Real agencies demand money on video call?

courses.title: Scams II: Ponzi schemes, fake trading apps, tips and romance-investment fraud
courses.summary: The arithmetic of impossible returns and the checklist that exposes investment scams.
outcomes: Show why 5% a month is impossible to sustain

scenes.text: A scheme promises 5% a month 'guaranteed' and shows early payouts.
A student checks what that means over a year.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice. No legitimate regulated product guarantees high returns.

steps.title: Compounding
steps.body: 5% a month compounds to 1.05^12 = 1.7959, i.e. about 79.6% a year, far beyond any sustainable return.

steps.title: Ponzi mechanics
steps.body: Early payouts come from new investors' money, so collapse is certain when inflows slow.

scenes.text: A group of 'experts' shares winning screenshots and invites Rahul to a 'VIP' app.
He checks who they are.

steps.title: Checks
steps.body: Is the adviser/broker on SEBI's registered lists? Is the app on the official exchange or broker list? Does it route funds only to the registered entity's account?

steps.title: Fake apps
steps.body: Fake apps show fabricated profits; withdrawals fail until you pay 'tax' or 'fees'.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: If you cannot verify registration, do not invest.

App from the official store linked on the broker's site

scenes.text: An online friend of three weeks recommends a crypto-trading platform and shows his profits.
Dia invests small, sees gains, then is urged to invest much more.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: Build trust, show fake profits, escalate deposits, block withdrawals with fees. Often called 'pig-butchering'.

steps.title: Defence
steps.body: Do not move money for someone you have not met; verify identity and platform independently; talk to someone you trust.

steps.title: If trapped
steps.body: Stop paying, keep chats, report on 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in. Shame helps scammers; report anyway.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment or insurance advice. Policy terms differ; read the policy document and ask a licensed adviser.

steps.title: Needs method
steps.body: Cover = debts + years of family expenses to replace − existing assets. The years figure is a planning choice.

activity.prompt: Debt ₹40 lakh, 10 years × ₹6 lakh expenses, assets ₹20 lakh. Cover needed (₹ lakh)?

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Premium ₹50,000 with cover ₹5 lakh = 10× premium. A term plan might give far larger cover for the same money; the quote depends on age and health.

steps.title: Disclosure

steps.title: Avoid

steps.title: Family

The policy has a 20% co-pay.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not insurance or medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor; in an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Co-pay
steps.body: A co-pay is the fixed share of an admissible claim you pay yourself.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 20% of 2,00,000 = ₹40,000 paid by the family; insurer pays ₹1,60,000, if the whole bill is admissible.

Other charges get reduced too.

steps.title: Proportionate deduction
steps.body: If the room is costlier than the limit, some policies reduce related charges in the ratio limit ÷ actual rent.

steps.title: Prevent
steps.body: Choose policies without room-rent caps if affordable; ask the hospital the category before admission.

activity.prompt: Limit ₹5,000/day, actual ₹8,000/day, doctor fees ₹40,000. Payable after proportionate deduction (₹)?

steps.title: Two routes

steps.title: Waiting periods
steps.body: Policies have initial and pre-existing-disease waiting periods; IRDAI rules also include a moratorium after continuous cover (currently five years; verify).

steps.title: Emergency
steps.body: In an emergency treat first; inform the insurer within the stated time.

a.text: Planned surgery at a network hospital. What do you do first?

courses.title: Motor insurance: third-party, own-damage, IDV and no-claim bonus
courses.summary: What motor policies cover, how IDV and NCB work and what to do after an accident.

scenes.text: Aman's car cost ₹10 lakh new.
At renewal the insurer shows an IDV lower than he expects.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not insurance advice. Check your policy and IRDAI rules.

steps.title: Cover types
steps.body: Third-party liability cover is mandatory under the Motor Vehicles Act. Own-damage cover (comprehensive) protects your own vehicle. IDV is the insured declared value, the maximum for total loss.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Standard depreciation on the vehicle's age: 1–2 years is 20%. IDV ≈ 10,00,000 × 0.80 = ₹8,00,000.

activity.prompt: New price ₹10 lakh, age 1.5 years, 20% depreciation. IDV (₹ lakh)?

scenes.text: Aman made no claims for three years.
His renewal premium falls.

steps.title: NCB
steps.body: NCB is a discount on the own-damage premium for claim-free years: 20%, 25%, 35%, 45%, 50% for years 1 to 5 (commonly used slabs; verify in your policy). Small claims may cost more NCB than they recover.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Own-damage premium ₹10,000, NCB 35% → ₹6,500.

steps.title: Portability
steps.body: NCB belongs to the owner and can move with them to a new policy or vehicle.

activity.prompt: Own-damage premium ₹10,000 with 35% NCB. Payable (₹)?

scenes.text: Another car hits Aman's car at a signal.
He must act correctly.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body: Ensure safety, call 112 if anyone is hurt, photograph the scene, exchange details, inform the insurer promptly and file an FIR where the law or the insurer requires it (for example third-party injury or theft).

steps.title: Do not
steps.body: Do not move a seriously injured person unless there is danger; do not admit fault at the scene.

steps.title: Surveyor
steps.body: The insurer sends a surveyor to assess damage.

scenes.text: A health claim is rejected citing a pre-existing condition.

steps.title: Escalation ladder

steps.title: Legal
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

uni-fin-markets-a.title: Stock market from zero – I: exchanges, demat, IPOs, analysis
uni-fin-markets-a.description: How Indian exchanges work, opening a demat account, IPO basics, fundamental ratio labs and technical-analysis concepts with a clear risk warning. Educational, not investment advice; markets can lose money.

courses.title: How stock exchanges work
courses.summary: Order books, bid-ask, matching, settlement and who regulates what.
outcomes: Compute the average price of a market order
Name the regulator and the depositories

scenes.text: Anil sees two columns of prices and quantities on a trading screen.
He does not know which side he would hit when buying.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice. It recommends no stock, fund or trade. Markets can lose money.

steps.title: Bid and ask
steps.body: Bids are buyers' offers; asks are sellers' prices. The gap is the spread. A buyer at market takes the cheapest asks first (price-time priority).

activity.prompt: Asks: 60 @ ₹100.10 and 80 @ ₹100.20. You market-buy 100 shares. Total cost (₹)?

options: Gap between best bid and ask

scenes.text: News hits and Anil places a market order on a thinly traded stock.
He is filled far from the last price.

steps.title: Order types
steps.body: A **limit order** sets your worst acceptable price; a **market order** accepts any price now. Illiquid shares have wide spreads.

steps.title: Settlement
steps.body: Indian equity cash trades settle on a T+1 basis (trade day plus one working day). Exchanges also use circuit limits to curb extreme moves.

steps.title: Regulation
steps.body: SEBI regulates markets; NSE and BSE are exchanges; NSDL and CDSL are depositories.

activity.prompt: Match term to meaning.

quiz.q: Who regulates securities markets in India?
quiz.why: Securities and Exchange Board of India.

options: Settlement one working day after trade

quiz.q: Illiquid stock spread tends to be?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – trace a trade from click to demat

scenes.text: Anil buys 10 shares through his broker.
He wants to know what happens after clicking buy.

steps.title: The chain
steps.body: Order → broker → exchange matching → clearing corporation guarantees settlement → depository moves shares into your demat account.

steps.title: Why it is safe
steps.body: Clearing corporations reduce counterparty risk; they do not protect you from price losses.

steps.title: Records
steps.body: Your broker's contract note and demat statement are your records.

activity.prompt: Order the life of a trade.
items: Broker routes it to the exchange

scenes.text: Kavya sees ads promising free demat accounts with tips groups.
She decides to check registration first.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice and recommends no broker or share.

steps.title: What you need
steps.body: PAN, Aadhaar-linked KYC, a bank account and e-sign. Choose a SEBI-registered broker and check the registration on SEBI's site.

steps.title: Compare charges
steps.body: Account opening, annual maintenance, brokerage, statutory charges and taxes all differ.

items: Check broker registration on SEBI's website
Complete KYC with PAN and Aadhaar
Place a tiny test order only after learning

scenes.text: An IPO is 20 times subscribed and social media is excited.
Kavya applies for one lot but may receive nothing.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: The DRHP/RHP and price band are in the offer documents. Subscription = bids ÷ shares offered. Oversubscribed categories use lottery-type allotment for retail.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Offered 1.2 crore shares; bids 24 crore → 20×. Issue ₹148, listing ₹170: gain = 22/148 = 14.86%.

steps.title: Listing gains are not guaranteed
steps.body: Some IPOs list below the issue price.

activity.prompt: Issue price ₹148, listing price ₹170. Listing gain % (2 decimals)?

scenes.text: A channel promises 'guaranteed listing profit'.
Kavya sorts claims into reasonable and red flags.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: Guarantees, pressure to pay a grey-market 'tip' fee, unregistered advisers and promises of fixed allotment.

steps.title: Reasonable checks
steps.body: Read the objects of the issue, promoters, financials, risk factors and valuation versus peers.

steps.title: Law
steps.body: Only SEBI-registered advisers may give investment advice for a fee.

courses.title: Fundamental analysis: ratio labs
courses.summary: Compute EPS, P/E, ROE, debt-to-equity and dividend yield from a worked company example.

scenes.text: Sundaram Foods (fictional) reports profit after tax of ₹500 crore with 50 crore shares.
Its share trades at ₹150.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice. The company is fictional and no valuation here is a recommendation.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: EPS = profit after tax ÷ shares. P/E = price ÷ EPS.

activity.prompt: PAT ₹500 crore, 50 crore shares, price ₹150. P/E?

lessons.title: Lab: ROE, debt-to-equity and dividend yield

scenes.text: Shareholders' equity is ₹2,500 crore and borrowings ₹1,000 crore.
The dividend is ₹3 per share.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: ROE = PAT ÷ equity. Debt-to-equity = borrowings ÷ equity. Dividend yield = dividend per share ÷ price.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Ratios use past data and accounting choices; look at trends and cash flow too.

activity.prompt: PAT ₹500 crore, equity ₹2,500 crore. ROE %?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – compare two fictional companies

scenes.text: Alpha (fictional) has P/E 25 and ROE 22%; Beta has P/E 12 and ROE 9%.
A learner asks which is better.

steps.title: No single winner
steps.body: A higher P/E can reflect higher quality or growth; a low P/E can signal problems. Compare growth, debt, cash flow and risk.

steps.title: Checklist
steps.body: Revenue growth, margins, ROE, debt, cash flow, governance, valuation.

steps.title: Not advice
steps.body: This comparison teaches method; it does not rank real companies.

a.text: Beta looks 'cheap' at P/E 12. What is the best next step?

choices.label: Buy because cheap
choices.feedback: Cheap can be cheap for reasons.

choices.label: Study why: debt, growth, cash flow, governance

b.text: You find falling margins and rising debt; the low P/E has a reason.

c.text: You ignored risks; learn the checklist first.

courses.title: Technical analysis concepts – with a clear risk warning
courses.summary: Moving averages, support/resistance and position sizing as concepts, and why charts do not predict the future.

scenes.text: A college club debates whether chart patterns predict prices.
They start with the simplest tool: an average.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice. Technical analysis is a set of ideas, not a guarantee; most active traders lose money. Never trade money you cannot afford to lose.

steps.title: Moving average
steps.body: A 5-day simple moving average (SMA) is the average of the last five closes. It smooths noise and lags.

scenes.text: A learner wants a rule limiting loss per trade.
A teacher shows the 1% risk idea (a teaching rule).

steps.title: Idea
steps.body: Decide the most you can lose on one idea first, then compute quantity. Quantity = risk amount ÷ (entry − stop).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Capital 5,00,000; risk 1% = 5,000; stop is ₹10 below entry → 500 shares.

steps.title: Gaps
steps.body: Prices can gap through a stop and losses can exceed plan.

activity.prompt: Capital ₹5,00,000, risk 1%, stop ₹10 below entry. Quantity?

quiz.q: Can price gap past a stop?

scenes.text: A tool shows a pattern that 'worked' on old data.
It fails live.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: Overfitting, costs, slippage, changing regimes and luck. A pattern that worked in hindsight may be noise.

steps.title: Costs add up
steps.body: Brokerage, taxes and spreads eat small edges.

steps.title: Risk
steps.body: Leveraged products amplify losses. Seek a SEBI-registered adviser for advice.

statements.s: A pattern that worked on past data is guaranteed to work again.
statements.why: Past performance does not guarantee future results.

options: Only what you can afford to lose

uni-fin-markets-b.title: Stock market from zero – II: funds, bonds, gold, REITs, derivatives
uni-fin-markets-b.description: Mutual funds and SIPs, index funds and ETFs, bonds, gold, REITs, derivatives risk and why most intraday traders lose. Educational, not investment advice; returns used are assumptions, not forecasts.

courses.title: Mutual funds and SIPs
courses.summary: NAV, units, expense ratio, SIP arithmetic and rupee-cost averaging.
outcomes: Compute SIP future value under an assumed return

scenes.text: Pooja invests ₹10,000 in a fund whose NAV is ₹25.
She is unsure what she actually owns.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice. Mutual fund investments are subject to market risks; read scheme documents.

steps.title: Units
steps.body: A fund pools money and issues units. NAV = (assets − liabilities) ÷ units. Units bought = amount ÷ NAV.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 10,000 ÷ 25 = 400 units. If NAV rises to 30, value = 12,000.

activity.prompt: Invest ₹10,000 at NAV ₹25. Units allotted?

scenes.text: Pooja sets up a monthly SIP of ₹5,000 for 10 years.
A calculator shows a number that depends on an assumed return.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: FV = P × ((1+i)^n − 1) ÷ i for month-end instalments, with i the monthly rate and n the months.

steps.title: Assumption
steps.body: 12% is an assumption for arithmetic, not a forecast. Real returns vary and can be negative.

activity.prompt: SIP ₹5,000 a month, 120 months, assumed 1% per month. FV in ₹ lakh (2 decimals)?

scenes.text: NAV is ₹10, ₹8, ₹12 in three months; Pooja invests ₹1,000 each month.
She computes her average cost.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Units: 100 + 125 + 83.33 = 308.33. Average cost = 3,000 ÷ 308.33 ≈ ₹9.73, below the simple average NAV of ₹10.

steps.title: What it does
steps.body: It reduces timing worry and builds discipline; it does not remove market risk or guarantee profit.

steps.title: Costs
steps.body: Check expense ratio and exit load. A 1% expense ratio on ₹10,00,000 is ₹10,000 a year.

activity.prompt: ₹1,000 each at NAV 10, 8, 12. Average cost per unit (₹, 2 decimals)?

questions.q: Rupee-cost averaging average cost vs average NAV?

courses.title: Index funds and ETFs
courses.summary: Passive investing, tracking error, ETF trading mechanics and cost comparison.

scenes.text: Two funds follow the same index; one charges 0.2% and another 1.5%.
Arjun wonders if the gap matters.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice and recommends no fund. Index funds fall when markets fall.

steps.title: Passive
steps.body: An index fund aims to match an index such as the Nifty 50 at low cost. Tracking error measures how closely it follows.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Cost gap 1.5% − 0.2% = 1.3% a year. On ₹10 lakh, that is ₹13,000 in year one.

activity.prompt: Corpus ₹10,00,000; cost gap 1.3% per year. Extra cost in year 1 (₹)?

scenes.text: An ETF's iNAV is ₹100 but it trades at ₹102.
Arjun asks why.

steps.title: How ETFs work
steps.body: ETFs trade on exchanges like shares. Market makers help keep price near NAV, but thin volume can create premiums or discounts.

steps.title: Practice
steps.body: Use limit orders and check volume and spread.

activity.prompt: ETF trades at ₹102 versus iNAV ₹100. Premium %?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – passive vs active checklist

scenes.text: Arjun lists what he must compare.
He finds cost, tracking and strategy.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Expense ratio, tracking error, index, fund size, liquidity (ETFs), taxation, your horizon.

steps.title: Active
steps.body: Active funds aim to beat an index but many fail after costs over long periods; compare with a benchmark.

steps.title: Taxation
steps.body: Tax rules change; check the current rules.

courses.title: Bonds, gold and REITs
courses.summary: How bond prices relate to yields, how gold behaves, and how REITs distribute income.

scenes.text: A bond of face value ₹1,000 pays an 8% coupon and trades at ₹950.
Riya compares the income to her price.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice. Bonds carry interest-rate, credit and liquidity risk.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: Coupon = face × rate. Current yield = coupon ÷ price. When market yields rise, existing bond prices fall.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Coupon = 1,000×8% = 80. Current yield = 80/950 = 8.42%.

activity.prompt: Face ₹1,000, coupon 8%, price ₹950. Current yield % (2 decimals)?

scenes.text: Riya's family holds gold for weddings.
She calculates a past return and asks about the future.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body: Gold pays no interest, can swing widely, and is often used as a diversifier. Options include jewellery, coins, gold ETFs and sovereign schemes when available. Check each product's regulation, charges and purity.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Price ₹50,000 → ₹62,000 per 10 g: return = 12,000/50,000 = 24%. Past gains do not predict future ones.

steps.title: Jewellery costs
steps.body: Making charges and resale deductions reduce returns.

activity.prompt: Gold ₹50,000 → ₹62,000 per 10 g. Return %?

scenes.text: A REIT owns offices and distributes rental income to unit holders.
Riya computes yield from a hypothetical ₹8 per unit on a ₹100 price.

steps.title: REITs
steps.body: A REIT pools income-producing real estate and trades like a share. SEBI rules require REITs to distribute most of their net distributable cash flows (90%); details are in SEBI's regulations.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Yield = 8/100 = 8%. Price and distributions can both fall.

steps.title: Risk
steps.body: Vacancies, rent resets, interest rates and liquidity all matter.

activity.prompt: Distribution ₹8 per unit, price ₹100 (hypothetical). Yield %?

courses.title: Derivatives risk and why most intraday traders lose
courses.summary: Futures and options risk, leverage arithmetic and the evidence that most individual short-term traders lose money.
outcomes: Explain option buyer and seller risk
Describe why short-term trading usually loses

scenes.text: Rohan controls a futures position worth ₹10,00,000 with margin of ₹1,20,000.
The market falls 5%.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment advice. Derivatives are high-risk instruments and losses can exceed the money you first put in. Numbers are hypothetical.

steps.title: Leverage
steps.body: Margin is a deposit, not the exposure. Gains and losses apply to the full notional.

activity.prompt: Notional ₹10,00,000; price falls 5%; margin ₹1,20,000. Loss as % of margin (1 decimal)?

scenes.text: A call option costs ₹100 premium; the assumed lot is 75 units (hypothetical; real lot sizes change).
It expires worthless.

steps.title: Buyer
steps.body: An option buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid; time decay works against the buyer.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Premium ₹100 × 75 = ₹7,500 lost if the option expires worthless.

steps.title: Seller
steps.body: An option seller collects a small premium but can face very large losses. Most expiring options end worthless, which is why selling looks safe until it is not.

activity.prompt: Premium ₹100, assumed lot 75. Maximum loss for the buyer (₹)?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – the arithmetic of losing

scenes.text: Meera wins 55 of 100 trades and still loses money.
Costs and the size of losses explain it.

steps.title: Expectancy
steps.body: Expectancy per trade = win rate × average win − loss rate × average loss − costs.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 0.55×₹800 = 440; 0.45×₹1,100 = 495; net = −55 per trade before costs. Add ₹60 costs: −115 per trade; ×100 trades = −₹11,500.

steps.title: Evidence
steps.body: SEBI's published studies on individual equity-derivatives (F&O) traders found that roughly nine in ten lost money in the periods studied, with costs adding to losses. Read SEBI's own reports for exact figures and years. Short-term trading is a hard, zero-sum-before-costs game.

activity.prompt: Win rate 55%, avg win ₹800, avg loss ₹1,100, costs ₹60 per trade. Total result over 100 trades (₹)?

options: Win rate, size of wins/losses, costs

questions.q: Win 60%, avg win 500, avg loss 600, no cost: expectancy?

uni-fin-tax.title: Income tax filing in India
uni-fin-tax.description: Old vs new regime, ITR forms in general terms, records and notices, plus a number-input calculator lab. Slabs used in labs are clearly stated illustrative assumptions; always check the current Income-tax Department rules. Educational, not tax or investment advice.

outcomes: Compute slab tax step by step

lessons.title: Lab: Slab tax step by step

scenes.text: Tanvi earns ₹10 lakh taxable and thinks the whole amount is taxed at one rate.
Her CA shows her that each band is taxed at its own rate.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not investment or tax advice. The slabs below are ILLUSTRATIVE assumptions for practice and ignore rebates, surcharge and changes made by recent Budgets. Check incometax.gov.in for current rates.

steps.title: Illustrative slabs (practice only)
steps.body: Assume: up to 3,00,000 nil; 3–6 lakh 5%; 6–9 lakh 10%; 9–12 lakh 15%; 12–15 lakh 20%; above 15 lakh 30%.

activity.prompt: Using the illustrative slabs, tax on ₹10,00,000 (before cess)? (₹)

options: Each band taxed at its own rate

quiz.why: Basic exemption in the practice slabs.

scenes.text: Sameer has home-loan interest, insurance and an 80C-type investment.
He is not sure whether claiming them beats lower rates.

steps.title: The trade-off
steps.body: One regime allows many deductions with higher rates; the other offers lower rates with few deductions. Which is cheaper depends on your deductions.

steps.title: Illustrative old slabs
steps.body: Assume old: up to 2.5 lakh nil; 2.5–5 lakh 5%; 5–10 lakh 20%; above 10 lakh 30%. Taxable 8 lakh: 12,500 + 3 lakh×20% (60,000) = 72,500.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Compute both, using your real deductions, and choose the lower. Re-check every year.

activity.prompt: Gross ₹10 lakh, deductions ₹2 lakh, illustrative OLD slabs. Tax on taxable ₹8 lakh? (₹)

scenes.text: Tanvi has gross ₹10 lakh and wants to know how many deductions make the old regime win.
She tests two cases.

steps.title: Case A
steps.body: Deductions 2 lakh: old tax 72,500 vs new 60,000. New wins (illustrative).

steps.title: Case B
steps.body: Deductions 3.5 lakh: taxable 6.5 lakh. Old: 12,500 + 1.5 lakh×20% (30,000) = 42,500 vs new 60,000. Old wins by 17,500.

steps.title: Lesson
steps.body: Larger genuine deductions tilt towards the old regime; but never buy a product only to save tax.

activity.prompt: Gross ₹10 lakh, deductions ₹3.5 lakh, illustrative OLD slabs. Tax? (₹)

courses.title: ITR forms in general terms and the filing workflow
courses.summary: Which kind of return suits which kind of income, and the usual steps of e-filing.
outcomes: Match income types to ITR forms in general terms

scenes.text: A salaried employee, a share trader, a freelance designer and a small shop owner each need a return.
They must pick the right form.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not tax or investment advice. Eligibility conditions and thresholds change; use the department's guidance.

steps.title: General idea
steps.body: ITR-1: simple salary/pension/one house/interest income within limits. ITR-2: no business income but more complex, such as capital gains. ITR-3: business or profession income. ITR-4: presumptive taxation for eligible small taxpayers.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: A wrong form may make the return defective.

activity.prompt: Match each person to the likely form (general terms).

scenes.text: Imran logs into the portal with his PAN.
He wants to be sure nothing is missed.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.body: Gather Form 16, interest certificates, AIS/Form 26AS, capital-gains statements and deduction proofs.

steps.title: File and verify
steps.body: File, then e-verify (for example with Aadhaar OTP, net banking or other available methods). A return is treated as filed validly only after verification within the permitted time.

steps.title: Deadlines
steps.body: Missing the due date can bring fees and interest; check the current due date for your category.

items: Choose regime and the right form

steps.title: Checklist idea
steps.body: Collect everything before opening the portal; mismatches between your records and AIS should be explained or reported.

steps.title: Keep copies

steps.title: No shortcuts
steps.body: Avoid agents promising inflated refunds; false claims bring penalties.

courses.title: The tax calculator lab: practise with stated assumptions
courses.summary: A hands-on calculator course with clearly stated illustrative slabs, cess and a marginal-rate lens.

lessons.title: Lab: Compute tax at ₹8, ₹12 and ₹14 lakh

scenes.text: Dev has offers at ₹8, ₹12 and ₹14 lakh taxable and wants to see how much extra he keeps.
He uses the practice slabs.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This is educational, not tax or investment advice. Slabs: nil to 3 lakh; 5% to 6 lakh; 10% to 9 lakh; 15% to 12 lakh; 20% to 15 lakh; 30% above. No rebate, surcharge or cess unless stated.

steps.title: Marginal rate
steps.body: Going from 12 to 14 lakh adds 40,000 tax on 2 lakh: 20% marginal rate.

activity.prompt: Tax on ₹14,00,000 with the stated slabs (₹)?

scenes.text: Dev's computation sheet has a line called health and education cess.
It is a percentage of the tax.

steps.title: Cess
steps.body: Health and education cess has been 4% of income tax (plus surcharge, if any). Verify the current figure.

steps.title: Order
steps.body: Compute tax, then surcharge if applicable, then cess on the sum, then subtract TDS and advance tax already paid.

activity.prompt: Tax on ₹12 lakh is ₹90,000. Add 4% cess. Total payable (₹)?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – average vs marginal rate at ₹20 lakh

scenes.text: Dev's pay rises to 20 lakh.
He wonders if he is taxed 30% on everything.

steps.title: Average rate
steps.body: 3,00,000 ÷ 20,00,000 = 15%, though the marginal rate is 30%.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Surcharge may apply to high incomes; it is ignored here.

activity.prompt: Tax on ₹20,00,000 with the stated slabs (₹)?

quiz.q: Is the whole income taxed at 30%?

lessons.title: Lab: TDS credit and balance tax

scenes.text: Neel's bank deducted tax on interest and his employer deducted TDS on salary.
He must find the balance.

steps.title: Educational, not investment advice
steps.body: This course is educational, not tax or investment advice. Figures are practice numbers.

steps.title: Credit
steps.body: TDS paid on your behalf is a credit visible in Form 26AS/AIS. Balance = total tax − TDS − advance tax.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Tax with cess 93,600; TDS 80,000; advance tax 0. Balance = 13,600.

activity.prompt: Total tax ₹93,600, TDS ₹80,000. Balance payable (₹)?

scenes.text: Pooja earns freelance income without TDS.
She may need to pay tax in instalments during the year.

steps.title: Dates
steps.body: Advance tax is generally due on 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March, with cumulative shares of 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% for those who pay it. Exemptions and special schemes exist; check the rules.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Estimated tax 80,000. By 15 Sep cumulative 45% = 36,000.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: Paying late can attract interest.

activity.prompt: Estimated annual tax ₹80,000. Cumulative advance tax due by 15 December at 75% (₹)?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – respond calmly to a notice

scenes.text: Neel gets a message saying his return has a mismatch.
He must not panic or ignore it.

steps.title: Check authenticity
steps.body: Verify through the official portal, not via links in unknown emails. Fake tax-refund messages are a common scam.

steps.title: Respond
steps.body: Read what is asked, gather proof, reply within the stated time, and consult a qualified tax professional if unsure.

steps.title: Never
steps.body: Never share OTP or card details to claim a refund.
